July 30 (Asia Today) -- South Korea's ruling and main opposition parties reached an agreement Thursday on legislation appointing an independent counsel to investigate ballot shortages and other alleged election-management failures during the June 3 local elections.

The parties also agreed to extend a parliamentary investigation into the National Election Commission by 30 days to allow additional examination of ballots and voting procedures, including those at a polling station in Seoul's Olympic Park.

Democratic Party floor leader Han Byung-do and People Power Party floor leader Chung Jeom-sig reached the agreement during a meeting at the National Assembly with the parties' senior deputy floor leaders.

The legislation will be formally titled the Act on the Appointment of an Independent Counsel to Investigate Suspected Violations of Voting Rights, Including the Ballot Shortage During the Ninth Nationwide Local Elections.

Democratic Party senior deputy floor leader Chun Jun-ho said the parties had resolved their principal differences over the scope and subjects of the investigation.

"The two parties have reached an agreement on the independent counsel legislation," Chun told reporters following the meeting.

The agreed provisions will be sent to the ruling and opposition members responsible for the National Assembly's Legislation and Judiciary Committee. They will draft the final statutory language based on the agreement.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_18763" });

Chun said most of the issues had been resolved and that the legislation was expected to be completed quickly.

People Power Party senior deputy floor leader Kim Seung-soo said the parties had previously agreed on the process for recommending an independent counsel but had continued negotiations over the investigation's scope.

"We have now reached agreement on the disputed issues after lengthy discussions," Kim said.

The parties agreed earlier this month to establish a six-member public recommendation committee, with each party selecting three members.

The committee would receive candidates recommended by the Korean Bar Association and the Korean Association of Law Schools. The parties would jointly select two candidates to submit to the president, who would appoint one of them as independent counsel.

The bill was scheduled to be considered first at Thursday's plenary session.

The session, originally scheduled for 2 p.m., was delayed until 3 p.m. to allow the Legislation and Judiciary Committee to complete its review of the bill.

Lawmakers were also expected to consider amendments to the Criminal Procedure Act that would eliminate prosecutors' supplementary investigative authority.

Another proposed amendment would shorten the review period for bills designated for fast-track consideration in the National Assembly.

The special investigation follows widespread criticism of election officials after polling stations ran short of ballots during the June 3 local elections, potentially preventing some voters from casting ballots or forcing them to wait for replacement supplies.

The parliamentary investigation committee has held hearings and questioned election officials over the shortages, ballot management and other alleged violations of voting rights.
